analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: 28 confirmed rabies cases in Harford County, matching last year’s total. Rabies vaccines are being offered at a significantly reduced cost to encourage pet owners to vaccinate their animals.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: A low-cost vaccine clinic is planned for October 24 at the Aberdeen Fire Department. Officials are urging pet owners to vaccinate their animals to prevent further spread.

news.title_zh: 哈福德县记录了 28 例 狂犬病 病例,计划设立低成本 疫苗 诊所 - WMAR 2 News 巴尔的摩
news.source_body_en: Harford County, Maryland, has recorded 28 confirmed rabies cases, matching the total from last year. An infected cat was found at the Humane Society, prompting officials to emphasize the importance of vaccination. In response, the Humane Society is organizing a low-cost vaccine clinic on October 24 at the Aberdeen Fire Department. This initiative aims to make rabies vaccinations more accessible, especially for pet owners facing financial challenges. Rabies vaccines are typically expensive, but the clinic offers them at a fraction of the cost, potentially saving hundreds of dollars. Officials warn that once symptoms appear, it is too late to treat rabies, underscoring the urgency of prevention. The event is part of ongoing efforts to combat the outbreak and protect both pets and humans from the deadly disease.

animal case of rabies WYSO | By Shay Frank Published October 1, 2026 at 2:26 PM EDT Facebook LinkedIn Email CDC / Public Domain Mosquitoes spread the West Nile virus. Clark County is investigating two infectious diseases including a human case of West Nile virus and a case of rabies in a bat. The human West Nile virus case is on the southern side of Elmwood Place in Springfield, while the rabid bat was found in the village of Medway in Bethel Township. Both cases of infectious disease are making their first appearance since 2021 in the county. West Nile virus is spread by infected mosquitoes that bite humans and rabies can be transmitted to humans by a variety of animals. Bats are the most common carriers of rabies and the only animals who have tested positive for rabies in Clark County in the last 20 years. West Nile virus cannot spread from person to person. The illness spread by mosquito also often goes undetected as 80% of infected people show no symptoms. If symptoms do show up for those exposed, they typically onset within three to fourteen days. Those include severe or mild fever, inflammation of the brain, head and body aches, vomiting, diarrhea, rash and swollen glands. Mild symptoms can last for a few days to a week. The Clark County Combined Health District said the best way to protect yourself is to prevent mosquito bites with EPA registered insect repellent. When outdoors, residents are encouraged to also wear loose-fitting, long sleeves and pants to protect from exposure. Residents can also prevent mosquitos around their home by emptying or covering items that hold water like buckets, tires, flowerpots, birdbaths and trash containers. If they cannot be emptied or discarded, residents can use products containing Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis to control mosquito larvae. the product is available at many garden and home improvement stores, About one in 150 people infected with the virus develop severe illness. Those symptoms include as high fever, headache, neck stiffness, muscle weakness, disorientation, tremors, seizures, paralysis, and coma. For rabies, exposure can come from a bite, scratch, direct skin contact with an infected animal and even sharing a room with that animal. Pet owners are encouraged to vaccinate their dogs and cats for rabies and keep domestic animals clear of all wildlife. If a bat is found near an unattended child or someone unable to communicate if exposure has occurred, exposure may have still happened. The resident who discovered the infected bat in Clark County has received life-saving post exposure prophylaxis. While rabies is rare in humans, it is always fatal once symptoms arise. If exposure has happened immediate medical care is critical. Officials said it is always best to capture the bat for testing but not to touch it with bare hands. People and pets should be kept away from the animal and doors or windows should be closed to limit escape. Once a bat is found and captured, residents should contact Clark County Health for guidance on testing it for rabies. The health department can be reached at 937-390-5600 or at info@clarkhealthohio.gov. Forgotten Password Cancel Home / Featured Content / Rabies Is on the Rise: Experts Offer Advice Rabies Is on the Rise: Experts Offer Advice Infectious disease experts weigh in on what to do if you think you’ve been exposed to rabies October 2, 2026 by University of Michigan Health Leave a Comment By Kelly Malcom Picture it: it’s the middle of the night and you’ve suddenly woken up to the sound of flapping wings. Somehow a bat has made its way into your home. Do you know what to do next? The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recently issued a health advisory for clinicians noting a nationwide increase in rabies exposure reports. According to the report, from July through August 2026, CDC received 17% more rabies-related inquiries than during the same period in 2025. “Rabies is an infection of the brain that is lethal in most mammals, including humans,” said Adam Lauring., M.D., Ph.D., head of the Division of Infectious Disease at Michigan Medicine, who recently had his own nighttime encounter with a bat. “Infected animals shed virus in their saliva, and it gains entry through breaks in skin or direct contact with mucus membranes. The virus then gains access to nerves and travels along the nerves toward the brain.” People are usually exposed via bites from infected animals, such as bats, raccoons, skunks or unvaccinated pets. Because there’s no treatment for rabies, management is focused on interrupting the virus’ ability to infiltrate the nervous system, because once that happens, it’s too late. Rabies “is 100% fatal – or nearly so – if the exposure is not managed appropriately,” said Lauring. Batty behavior “If you wake up with a bat in your room, you can’t rule out a bite or scratch while you were sleeping (even if you don’t see one). So, you should contact the health department and/or animal control for trapping/testing/or recommendations,” said Lauring. “In my case, I was so freaked out, I opened the window and ran out of the room, so we couldn’t test the bat. So, I needed to proceed with post exposure prophylaxis,” he said. The good news is you have some time after an animal exposure, says Laraine Washer, M.D., who consulted with Lauring following his encounter. “In most cases, rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, known as PEP, is a medical urgency, not an emergency. You can normally wait 48-72 hours to determine whether an animal is available for testing or observation.” Unfortunately, you can’t always rely on an animal’s behavior to tell whether it’s infected with rabies. “Specialized testing of the animal in a public health laboratory is typically required to determine if it had rabies.” But there can be some clues, including daytime activity in a nocturnal animal or an animal attacking without provocation, says Lauring. You’ve been bitten by an animal. What do you do? If you are bitten, wash the wound with soap and water and seek medical care. Depending on the severity and type of bite, a visit to urgent care or an emergency department may be required, says Washer, for a tetanus shot and depending on rabies reports in your area, rabies immunoglobulin and the first dose of rabies vaccine. Rabies PEP includes four total visits for vaccine doses. Michigan law requires that animal bites are immediately reported to the local health department. Thankfully, rodents like squirrels, hamsters, mice, and rabbits are unlikely to have rabies in the United States and public health officials are unlikely to recommend PEP for those types of bites. Whether rabies prophylaxis treatment is required for bites from pets, such as dogs, cats, and ferrets depends on whether they’ve been vaccinated. “Clinicians should consult with local or state public health officials when there are questions about whether PEP is indicated,” said Washer. Bottom line is when in doubt, say Michigan Medicine experts, seek medical attention following exposure to bats or when bitten by an animal. Sign up for Health Lab newsletters today. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 3, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Older Adults Delay Seeking Rabies Treatment After Animal Bites, Hangzhou Study Finds by Bioengineer October 2, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Rabies remains one of the deadliest infectious diseases known to medicine, with a case fatality rate that approaches 100 percent once clinical symptoms appear. Yet the disease is almost entirely preventable if exposed individuals receive timely post-exposure prophylaxis, a regimen of vaccination and, in higher-risk cases, immunoglobulin administration that can stop the virus before it reaches the nervous system. A new retrospective study from Hangzhou, China, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, has now added an important piece to the puzzle of why some people fail to access this lifesaving care promptly, and the answer points squarely at age. Researchers led by Zheng Yang of the Emergency Department at Tongde Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated with Zhejiang Chinese Medical University, analyzed 3,327 exposure-related clinic presentations recorded between October 2022 and October 2025. The team began with a larger pool of records and applied rigorous exclusion criteria, removing seven system-test entries, fifteen exposures classified as World Health Organization Category I, thirteen confirmed continuation visits, ten records with contradictory dates, and two unresolved duplicates. What remained was a clean hospital-based cohort suitable for examining two distinct questions: how quickly patients presented after a potential rabies exposure, and whether they had attempted any wound care on their own before arriving at the clinic. The central finding concerns timing. Of the 3,327 presentations, 218, or 6.6 percent, occurred on a calendar day after the day of injury. Because the study relied on electronic medical records rather than precise timestamps, the researchers used a date-based operational proxy for delay: presenting on a subsequent calendar day rather than the same day. This is a conservative measure, and the authors are careful to frame it as such, but it captures a meaningful gap in access to care. Rabies virus travels along peripheral nerves at a relatively slow rate, and every hour of delay before prophylaxis begins extends the window during which the virus could, in principle, establish itself at the wound site and begin its ascent. When the researchers fitted multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for other characteristics, patients aged 65 and older had significantly higher adjusted odds of subsequent-calendar-day presentation compared with the reference group aged 15 to 44 years. The adjusted odds ratio was 2.28, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.31 to 3.96 and a P value of 0.003. In practical terms, older adults in this cohort were more than twice as likely to show up at the clinic only after the calendar day of their exposure had passed. This age-related pattern persisted even after accounting for other variables in the model, suggesting that advancing age itself, or factors closely tied to it, creates a genuine barrier to prompt care-seeking after an animal bite or scratch. The study also examined pre-hospital wound management, the self-directed cleaning or treatment that patients perform before reaching professional care. Guidelines from the World Health Organization emphasize immediate and thorough washing of bite wounds with soap and running water for at least fifteen minutes, a simple intervention that mechanically reduces viral load at the exposure site. The researchers modeled any pre-hospital wound self-treatment as a separate binary outcome. Interestingly, the estimate for the oldest age group pointed in the opposite direction: patients aged 65 and older appeared less likely to report any self-treatment, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.71 and a confidence interval of 0.50 to 1.01. However, this estimate did not reach the conventional threshold of statistical significance, with a P value of 0.056, and the authors explicitly caution that it is imprecise and requires confirmation in future work. A methodologically important point in the paper is that the two outcomes were modeled separately. The authors stress that their analysis does not establish a combined individual-level outcome linking delay and self-treatment within the same patient. In other words, the data cannot tell us whether an older adult who delays presentation is also the same person who skips wound washing, or whether these behaviors occur independently across the cohort. This distinction matters for intervention design: if delay and inadequate wound care cluster in the same individuals, targeted outreach could address both at once, whereas independent patterns might require broader, population-level messaging. Two other associations emerged from the models. Patients who reported any pre-hospital wound self-treatment had higher adjusted odds of subsequent-calendar-day presentation, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.72 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 2.00 to 3.69. One plausible interpretation is that people who attempt self-care may believe they have managed the problem adequately and therefore postpone professional evaluation, though the observational design of the study prevents any firm causal claim. The temporal pattern of the data also revealed that presentations during the clinic-opening calendar period of October through December 2022 were associated with subsequent-calendar-day presentation, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.54. The authors interpret this finding as exploratory, noting that it may reflect the establishment phase of the clinic itself, shifts in case mix, seasonality of animal exposures, or unmeasured access factors rather than any stable behavioral pattern. The implications for rabies control programs, particularly in China where dog-mediated rabies persists at low but nonzero levels, are significant. Older adults represent a vulnerable population on multiple fronts. They may have reduced mobility, limited awareness of modern PEP protocols, greater reliance on traditional remedies, or fewer social contacts who can urge them to seek care quickly. Sensory and cognitive changes can also affect how seriously a minor bite wound is perceived. Because the incubation period of rabies can range from weeks to months depending on the site and severity of exposure, a delay of even one day is unlikely to be decisive in every case, but the cumulative effect of late presentation across a population contributes to preventable deaths. Public health campaigns that specifically target older adults, perhaps through community health workers, primary care touchpoints, or family-centered messaging, could help close this gap. The study’s design has limitations that the authors acknowledge. As a retrospective, single-center, hospital-based analysis, it captures only people who eventually reached the clinic, leaving unexamined the experiences of exposed individuals who never sought care at all. The date-based proxy for delay is coarser than exact time-to-presentation measurements, and self-reported wound treatment is subject to recall bias. The clinic-opening period association is explicitly flagged as potentially confounded by factors the data cannot disentangle. Nevertheless, the large cohort size, careful data cleaning, and transparent statistical reporting give the findings credibility, and the consistency of the age effect with prior studies cited in the paper’s supplementary comparisons, including work from Hangzhou and Wuhan, strengthens the case that delayed presentation among older adults is a reproducible phenomenon rather than a local artifact. Funded by the Zhejiang Provincial Bureau of Disease Control and Prevention Science and Technology Program, the study received ethics approval from Tongde Hospital of Zhejiang Province and was conducted on de-identified electronic medical record data with a waiver of informed consent, in accordance with the 2013 Declaration of Helsinki. As rabies continues to kill an estimated tens of thousands of people worldwide each year, most of them in Asia and Africa, research of this kind translates a grim global statistic into actionable local insight. The message for clinicians and health communicators is clear: when it comes to rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, age is not just a demographic variable but a risk factor for the behaviors that allow a preventable disease to claim lives. Ensuring that older adults recognize exposures as emergencies, wash wounds immediately, and reach prophylaxis clinics without delay may prove one of the most cost-effective interventions available in the ongoing effort to eliminate rabies deaths. The team began with a larger pool of records and applied rigorous exclusion criteria, removing seven system-test entries, fifteen exposures classified as World Health Organization Category I, thirteen confirmed continuation visits, ten records with contradictory dates, and two unresolved duplicates. What remained was a clean hospital-based cohort suitable for examining two distinct questions: how quickly patients presented after a potential rabies exposure, and whether they had attempted any wound care on their own before arriving at the clinic. The central finding concerns timing. Of the 3,327 presentations, 218, or 6.6 percent, occurred on a calendar day after the day of injury. Because the study relied on electronic medical records rather than precise timestamps, the researchers used a date-based operational proxy for delay: presenting on a subsequent calendar day rather than the same day. This is a conservative measure, and the authors are careful to frame it as such, but it captures a meaningful gap in access to care. Rabies virus travels along peripheral nerves at a relatively slow rate, and every hour of delay before prophylaxis begins extends the window during which the virus could, in principle, establish itself at the wound site and begin its ascent. When the researchers fitted multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for other characteristics, patients aged 65 and older had significantly higher adjusted odds of subsequent-calendar-day presentation compared with the reference group aged 15 to 44 years. The adjusted odds ratio was 2.28, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.31 to 3.96 and a P value of 0.003. In practical terms, older adults in this cohort were more than twice as likely to show up at the clinic only after the calendar day of their exposure had passed. This age-related pattern persisted even after accounting for other variables in the model, suggesting that advancing age itself, or factors closely tied to it, creates a genuine barrier to prompt care-seeking after an animal bite or scratch. The study also examined pre-hospital wound management, the self-directed cleaning or treatment that patients perform before reaching professional care. Guidelines from the World Health Organization emphasize immediate and thorough washing of bite wounds with soap and running water for at least fifteen minutes, a simple intervention that mechanically reduces viral load at the exposure site. The researchers modeled any pre-hospital wound self-treatment as a separate binary outcome. Interestingly, the estimate for the oldest age group pointed in the opposite direction: patients aged 65 and older appeared less likely to report any self-treatment, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.71 and a confidence interval of 0.50 to 1.01. However, this estimate did not reach the conventional threshold of statistical significance, with a P value of 0.056, and the authors explicitly caution that it is imprecise and requires confirmation in future work. A methodologically important point in the paper is that the two outcomes were modeled separately. The authors stress that their analysis does not establish a combined individual-level outcome linking delay and self-treatment within the same patient. In other words, the data cannot tell us whether an older adult who delays presentation is also the same person who skips wound washing, or whether these behaviors occur independently across the cohort. This distinction matters for intervention design: if delay and inadequate wound care cluster in the same individuals, targeted outreach could address both at once, whereas independent patterns might require broader, population-level messaging. Two other associations emerged from the models. Patients who reported any pre-hospital wound self-treatment had higher adjusted odds of subsequent-calendar-day presentation, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.72 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 2.00 to 3.69. One plausible interpretation is that people who attempt self-care may believe they have managed the problem adequately and therefore postpone professional evaluation, though the observational design of the study prevents any firm causal claim. The temporal pattern of the data also revealed that presentations during the clinic-opening calendar period of October through December 2022 were associated with subsequent-calendar-day presentation, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.54. The authors interpret this finding as exploratory, noting that it may reflect the establishment phase of the clinic itself, shifts in case mix, seasonality of animal exposures, or unmeasured access factors rather than any stable behavioral pattern. The implications for rabies control programs, particularly in China where dog-mediated rabies persists at low but nonzero levels, are significant. Older adults represent a vulnerable population on multiple fronts. They may have reduced mobility, limited awareness of modern PEP protocols, greater reliance on traditional remedies, or fewer social contacts who can urge them to seek care quickly. Sensory and cognitive changes can also affect how seriously a minor bite wound is perceived. Because the incubation period of rabies can range from weeks to months depending on the site and severity of exposure, a delay of even one day is unlikely to be decisive in every case, but the cumulative effect of late presentation across a population contributes to preventable deaths. Public health campaigns that specifically target older adults, perhaps through community health workers, primary care touchpoints, or family-centered messaging, could help close this gap. The study’s design has limitations that the authors acknowledge. As a retrospective, single-center, hospital-based analysis, it captures only people who eventually reached the clinic, leaving unexamined the experiences of exposed individuals who never sought care at all. The date-based proxy for delay is coarser than exact time-to-presentation measurements, and self-reported wound treatment is subject to recall bias. The clinic-opening period association is explicitly flagged as potentially confounded by factors the data cannot disentangle. Nevertheless, the large cohort size, careful data cleaning, and transparent statistical reporting give the findings credibility, and the consistency of the age effect with prior studies cited in the paper’s supplementary comparisons, including work from Hangzhou and Wuhan, strengthens the case that delayed presentation among older adults is a reproducible phenomenon rather than a local artifact. Funded by the Zhejiang Provincial Bureau of Disease Control and Prevention Science and Technology Program, the study received ethics approval from Tongde Hospital of Zhejiang Province and was conducted on de-identified electronic medical record data with a waiver of informed consent, in accordance with the 2013 Declaration of Helsinki. As rabies continues to kill an estimated tens of thousands of people worldwide each year, most of them in Asia and Africa, research of this kind translates a grim global statistic into actionable local insight. The message for clinicians and health communicators is clear: when it comes to rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, age is not just a demographic variable but a risk factor for the behaviors that allow a preventable disease to claim lives. Ensuring that older adults recognize exposures as emergencies, wash wounds immediately, and reach prophylaxis clinics without delay may prove one of the most cost-effective interventions available in the ongoing effort to eliminate rabies deaths. news.source_body_en: A study published in BMC Infectious Diseases on October 2, 2026, found that older adults in Hangzhou, China, are more likely to delay seeking rabies treatment after animal bites compared to younger adults. The research, led by Zheng Yang at Tongde Hospital, analyzed 3,327 clinic presentations between October 2022 and October 2025. Using a date-based proxy for delay, the study found that 6.6% of cases were presented on a subsequent calendar day. Older adults had an adjusted odds ratio of 2.28 for delayed presentation, suggesting they are more than twice as likely to delay care. The study also noted that older adults were less likely to perform pre-hospital wound self-treatment, though this finding was not statistically significant. The authors emphasized that the data cannot determine if these behaviors are linked, and they called for targeted public health campaigns to address this gap in care-seeking behavior among older adults.
news.content_zh: 2026 年 10 月 2 日发表在《BMC Infectiousdies》上的一项研究发现,与年轻人相比,中国杭州的老年人在被动物咬伤后更有可能推迟寻求 狂犬病 治疗。这项由同德医院郑阳领导的研究分析了 2022 年 10 月至 2025 年 10 月期间的 3,327 例临床就诊。研究使用基于日期的延迟代理,发现 6.6% 的病例在随后的日历日就诊。老年人延迟就诊的调整后优势比为 2.28,这表明他们延迟就诊的可能性是老年人的两倍多。该研究还指出,老年人不太可能进行院前伤口自我 治疗,尽管这一发现在统计上并不显着。作者强调,数据无法确定这些行为是否存在关联,他们呼吁开展有针对性的公共卫生活动,以解决老年人寻求护理行为的这一差距。

news.content_title: Dr. Bonnie Franklin: Rabies Is Still a Real Threat, So Why Doesn’t Santa Barbara County Require Cat Vaccinations?
news.content: Rabies is a fatal virus disease that attacks the central nervous system in mammals, including humans. It is not a disease that was only active historically. Worldwide, rabies causes about 59,000 human deaths annually. About 4,500 cases of rabies are detected in animals annually in the United States. This year in California, there have been 213 cases through mid-August. Of the confirmed rabies cases, 194 were bats,18 were skunks and one was a dog. In Santa Barbara County so far, there have been four confirmed cases of rabies in bats in 2026. In the United States we are finding rabies in mammals that were typically not observed to have rabies. In May, police in a suburban area of New Jersey responded to Lake Henry where an 8-year-old boy had been fishing from the shoreline when a beaver came out of the water and charged him. The boy tried to run away but tripped and fell. The beaver bit the boy, and the same beaver attacked multiple people at the lake. The beaver tested positive for rabies. There have also been confirmed cases of rabid beavers in Maryland and New York this year. In August, four goats from a traveling petting zoo tested positive following stops in Durham County, North Carolina. A rabid skunk had entered the goat’s enclosure and bit them. The goats then traveled to about 10 different stops across six North Carolina counties. Because they were baby goats, visitors often cuddled, pet and bottle fed them. Anyone who held or handled the goats may have been exposed to rabies. According to the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, exposed people are in the hundreds so far this year. California does not require cats to be vaccinated against rabies. Why? I am not sure. Cats are two times more likely to contract rabies than dogs or cattle. Your cat can get rabies from fighting with an aggressive rabid skunk or being bitten by or eating a rabid bat. When a bat gets rabies, it eventually falls to the ground and flails around with seizures. Cats see them as play toys. Cats may play with sick bats on the floor inside a house, as well as on the ground outside. You would never know if your outdoor cat encountered a rabid bat. The bite of a rabid bat leaves a very small puncture that typically is not apparent to owners nor is it painful to the cat. You cannot tell if a bat has rabies just by looking at it. Rabies can only be confirmed in a laboratory. Any bat that is active during the day or is found in a place where bats are not usually seen — like in your home or on your lawn — might be rabid. A bat that is unable to fly and is easily approached could be sick. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that if you find a bat that is sick or dead inside or outside your house talk to a healthcare or public health professional and have the bat captured or picked up for possible rabies testing. According the CDC, bats are one of the most commonly reported rabid animals in the United States and are the leading cause of rabies deaths in people. Rabid bats have been found in 49 states, with only Hawai‘i being rabies-free. The good news is that most bats do not have rabies. A single bat can eat thousands of insects every night, including mosquitos and the moth stage of damaging caterpillars that strip avocado leaves. They also are nocturnal pollinators of our cherished avocados here in Santa Barbara County. Although rabies vaccinations are required for dogs, Santa Barbara County does not require cats to be vaccinated against rabies in its unincorporated communities. All eight incorporated cities — Buellton, Carpinteria, Goleta, Guadalupe, Lompoc, Santa Barbara, Santa Maria and Solvang — do require rabies vaccines for any cat over the age of 4 months old. Indoor or outdoor cats need vaccination, as there are indoor and outdoor bats in their environment. Unfortunately, the county does not require rabies vaccines for cats in unincorporated areas, including Hope Ranch, Isla Vista, Los Alamos, Los Olivos, Montecito, Orcutt, Santa Ynez and Summerland. Maybe someone should ask Santa Barbara County why. MORE BONNIE FRANKLIN DVM

Franklin notes that rabies can be transmitted through bites or contact with infected animals, such as rabid bats or skunks, and that cats are more likely to contract rabies than dogs or cattle. She stresses the importance of contacting healthcare professionals if a bat is found in unusual locations, as rabies can only be confirmed in a laboratory. news.content_zh: 邦妮·富兰克林 (Bonnie Franklin) 博士对加利福尼亚州圣巴巴拉县 狂犬病 的持续威胁表示担忧,尽管对于非建制地区的猫缺乏强制性的 狂犬病 狂犬病。她强调,狂犬病 是一种致命病毒,影响包括人类在内的哺乳动物,并且不仅限于历史事件。在全球范围内,狂犬病 每年导致约 59,000 人死亡,而在美国,每年报告约 4,500 例动物病例。截至 2026 年 8 月中旬,加利福尼亚州已确诊 213 例 狂犬病 病例,其中 194 例涉及蝙蝠、18 例臭鼬和一只狗。圣巴巴拉县在 2026 年记录了四例确诊的蝙蝠 狂犬病 病例。富兰克林指出,狂犬病 可以通过咬伤或接触受感染的动物(例如患有狂犬病的蝙蝠或臭鼬)传播,并且猫比狗或牛更容易感染 狂犬病。她强调,如果在不寻常的地方发现蝙蝠,联系医疗保健专业人员的重要性,因为 狂犬病 只能在实验室中确认。文章还引用了新泽西州、马里兰州和北卡罗来纳州的 狂犬病 案例,其中一只患有狂犬病的海狸袭击了多人,而患有狂犬病的臭鼬在宠物动物园中暴露了山羊,导致数百人可能受到感染。富兰克林质疑为什么圣巴巴拉县不对非建制地区的猫要求 狂犬病 疫苗接种,并强调需要采取此类措施来保护宠物和人。

Working at KBIA Reports and Public Files Contact Us Tax ID number Missouri News An increase in rabies exposure spreads across Missouri KBIA | By KJ Drazen, Columbia Missourian Published October 2, 2026 at 8:08 AM CDT Facebook Bluesky Twitter LinkedIn Email The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issued an official health alert due to an increase of reports in human exposure to rabid or possibly rabid animals, according to the CDC’s website. The CDC has received 17% more rabies inquiries from July through August 2026 than it did during the same time period in 2025, according to the center’s website. Exposures to this disease have been coming from known rabies vectors as well as animals that it is less commonly seen in. Normally, rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms begin, according to the CDC. However, it is preventable if rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (rPEP) is administered to the patient before their symptoms start. Kevin Meyers, the animal control specialist for Columbia/Boone County Department of Public Health and Human Services, said rPEP is a series of four shots, administered on days zero, three, seven and 14, with a success rate of 100% as long as it is given prior to symptoms starting. To date, there have been 36 confirmed animal rabies cases across Missouri in 2026. The main transmitters in the state have been bats and skunks, according to the Missouri Department of Health’s website. But these treatments — while necessary for survival — do not come without a cost. “The cost of treatment is incredibly high, usually ranging between $11,000 to $14,000 per person,” Meyers said. Meyers also provided information people should know to help keep these exposure numbers low. First of all, he said, make sure to have all pets vaccinated by a licensed veterinarian and keep them up to date on immunizations as they need renewal. If you are bitten by an animal, keep an eye on the animal for 10 days after the bite occurs, Meyers said. If the animal is still alive and healthy after those 10 days, there is no risk that it can spread the virus. Finally, do not touch wildlife. If an animal is found that needs to be relocated, contact Animal Control so they can remove it as soon as possible, Meyers said. If you have been bitten or believe you have been exposed, Animal Control can send a sample for rabies testing. “Sending off a sample is the only way to know with 100% certainty whether or not the animal was carrying the rabies virus,” Meyers said. The cost of treatment is high, typically ranging from $11,000 to $14,000 per person.

news.content_title: 'Rabies risk is real': Potential exposures to viral disease surging across BC
news.content: British Columbia has seen a spike in potential human rabies exposures in 2026, with 1,598 potential exposures compared with 931 potential exposures in 2025, according to the BC Centre for Disease Control, or BCCDC. A potential human rabies exposure means there’s a risk that a person has been exposed to rabies, so they receive treatment to prevent the disease from developing. This number may capture people who were exposed to animals who did not carry the disease but were given treatment just to be safe. A person is considered to have rabies once they start showing symptoms. Once this happens there is no treatment. The disease is nearly always fatal, with a few very rare exceptions. Over the last 104 years there have been only 28 human rabies cases in Canada, the BCCDC said. Two of them were in B.C. Rabies deaths are much higher in countries with higher incidences of dog bites, in particular in poorer, more rural communities that don’t have adequate access to post-exposure treatment. The United States is also reporting an increase in potential human rabies exposures this year, but not an increase in rabies cases. Photo credit: Cory Olson/WCS Canada It’s not clear if the increase in potential exposures is because more people are coming into contact with potentially infected animals or if there’s more public awareness about the importance of seeking medical attention after potential exposure, the BCCDC said in an emailed statement. The number of rabies cases in bats does not appear to be increasing, so “there is no reason to believe there is an increased risk of rabies infection” in B.C. or elsewhere in Canada, the BCCDC said. In B.C. any physical contact with a bat is considered an exposure because one in 200 bats can carry rabies. If the bat is captured, is tested and is negative, it is no longer considered an exposure. Bats are the only wild animal in B.C. that carries the disease and is not killed by it. In the Prairies, skunks can carry rabies. In Eastern Canada, racoons and foxes also carry the disease, and in parts of the United States opossums can live with the disease, Heather James, a small-animal veterinarian in Prince George and a board member of the Society of BC Veterinarians, told The Tyee. Symptoms can take three to eight weeks to develop after exposure. Once symptoms start, the disease is always fatal in humans and pets, James said. But medical intervention can prevent the disease from developing. After a potential exposure, the wound or area of contact should immediately be washed with soap and water for at least 15 minutes, according to HealthLink BC. Next, a person should seek immediate care from a health-care provider, who will assess and decide if the person needs rabies immune globulin and/or the rabies vaccine. If administered early, these measures almost always prevent a person from developing rabies. The BCCDC recommends that bat researchers, veterinarians and other people who may come in contact with the virus get the rabies pre-exposure vaccine. In B.C. there are no provincial rabies vaccine mandates, the BCCDC said. Some employers may, however, require vaccines as part of occupational health and safety policies. In Ontario and parts of the United States, rabies vaccines are mandatory for pets, James said. In B.C., many veterinary hospitals, boarding facilities and groomers will also require pets to be vaccinated to protect staff, she added. Public awareness about rabies is high right now because of a CBC article published this summer about an 11-year-old boy in Ontario who died from rabies in 2024, the BCCDC said. There are no other trends in bat and animal populations that would help explain the increase in potential rabies exposures, it added. Rabies vaccines for pets The American Animal Hospital Association recommends that all pets, regardless of whether they are indoor or outdoor pets, be vaccinated against rabies, James said. This protects pets if a bat ever gets in the home, or if a cat or dog comes home with a bat in its mouth. When a pet comes home with a bat, it’s recommended to take the bat to a veterinarian so it can be tested for rabies. Over the summer this process identified two bats, brought home by cats, that had rabies in Courtenay and Campbell River, said Leanne Kelly, a registered veterinary technologist at Van Isle Veterinary Hospital. The cats were given post-exposure treatment and did not develop rabies, but the cases have created a spike in pet owners wanting to vaccinate their pets against the disease, Kelly said. Many pet owners will vaccinate their pets but skip the rabies vaccine because they don’t think it’s necessary, she said. She estimates that over the summer her clinic saw a 20 per cent increase in pet owners asking for their pets to be vaccinated and a 20 per cent increase in pet owners calling to ask if the rabies vaccine is available. “I think it’s going to continue to go up as people get more and more aware that the rabies risk is real,” she said. While people occasionally post misinformation about pet vaccines on social media, veterinarians and vet techs in Prince George, Courtenay and Kelowna told The Tyee they rarely meet pet owners who are outright hostile to them or refuse all vaccines for their pets. Most people are just “conflicted” and overwhelmed by all of the information, and misinformation, on the internet, James said. Pet owners will say they’re worried the antigen in the vaccine can cause an allergic reaction in their pet, she said. But that’s misrepresenting the situation a little. An antigen is any substance that can be recognized by an immune system. Antigens are in everything, including cheeseburgers, vaccines and toothpaste. An immune system decides to react or not react every time it is exposed to an antigen, and it is exposed to thousands of antigens every day. There’s only one antigen in a rabies vaccine for the body to potentially react to, which is a fraction of the number of antigens in a cheeseburger, James added. James and Kelly said breeders seem to be a source of pet vaccine misinformation, telling new pet owners what vaccines they should and shouldn’t give their pets. However, pet owners are generally open to talk with veterinarians about their concerns, and the majority of them fully vaccinate their pets. Marco Veenis, a veterinarian at Okanagan Veterinary Hospital who has been practising since 1988, said he’s seen vaccine hesitancy growing over the last decade. He said this is likely due to the rise of social media and online misinformation. Patients will say they don’t believe in vaccines, but when you ask them why, they don’t have an answer, he said. Vets will recommend vaccines based on a pet’s lifestyle, for example if they go to a dog park or travel internationally, Veenis said, but ultimately it’s up to the pet owner to decide what shots their pet gets. “It’s not my job to tell them what to do. It’s my job to make sure they can make a properly informed decision,” he added. James said it’s recommended that puppies and kittens be vaccinated for rabies when they are as young as three months old, again at one year and then every three years. The vaccine costs about $30. With a vet fee and other charges, for example the cost of other vaccines, a visit may cost between $125 and $200. James has seen rabies in cats and dogs, and in horses and cattle when she worked in Saskatchewan. “Sometimes they can’t swallow or walk,” she said. “It’s just really scary.” If an unvaccinated pet is potentially exposed to rabies, a vet will follow BCCDC guidelines to determine if the pet can be given a post-exposure vaccine, if they need to quarantine the pet or if they must euthanize it. Pet owners and people who came in contact with the pet will also have to be assessed by a health-care provider. The province’s rabies protocols are ultimately designed to keep humans safe. “We don’t want to lose our cats or dogs,” she said, “but at the end of the day it’s a different kind of tragic when a human dies of rabies.” Another vaccine-preventable illness that’s becoming more common is leptospirosis, a bacterial disease that causes kidney and liver failure. Leptospirosis tends to have more serious consequences for dogs than it has for cats. The disease is not as common in cats. Leptospirosis is transmitted through wildlife or rat urine. The American Animal Hospital Association recently declared the vaccine for leptospirosis to be a “core” vaccine for dogs because of its increasing prevalence, James said. No leptospirosis vaccine is currently available for cats. Outdoor cats are more likely to contract leptospirosis than indoor cats, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Leptospirosis can transfer to humans, where it can also cause kidney and liver failure. If you appreciate what we do, we ask that you consider supporting our local independent news platform. If you get value from KelownaNow and believe local independent media is important to our community we ask that you please consider subscribing to our daily newsletter. The province’s rabies protocols are ultimately designed to keep humans safe. “We don’t want to lose our cats or dogs,” she said, “but at the end of the day it’s a different kind of tragic when a human dies of rabies.” Another vaccine-preventable illness that’s becoming more common is leptospirosis, a bacterial disease that causes kidney and liver failure. Leptospirosis tends to have more serious consequences for dogs than it has for cats. The disease is not as common in cats. Leptospirosis is transmitted through wildlife or rat urine. The American Animal Hospital Association recently declared the vaccine for leptospirosis to be a “core” vaccine for dogs because of its increasing prevalence, James said. No leptospirosis vaccine is currently available for cats. Outdoor cats are more likely to contract leptospirosis than indoor cats, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Leptospirosis can transfer to humans, where it can also cause kidney and liver failure. If you appreciate what we do, we ask that you consider supporting our local independent news platform. If you get value from KelownaNow and believe local independent media is important to our community we ask that you please consider subscribing to our daily newsletter. Send your comments, news tips, typos, letter to the editor, photos and videos to news@kelownanow.com. news.content_zh: 据不列颠哥伦比亚省疾病控制中心 (BCCDC) 称,不列颠哥伦比亚省报告称,2026 年人类潜在 狂犬病 暴露病例将显着增加,从 2025 年的 931 例增至 1,598 例。正如 BCCDC 声明中指出的那样,这种上升可能归因于与受感染动物的更多实际接触或公众意识的提高。BCCDC 强调,蝙蝠中的 狂犬病 病例数量并未增加,表明感染风险并未增加。一旦出现 狂犬病 的症状,这种疾病几乎总是致命的,但早期的医疗干预可以预防它。BCCDC 建议蝙蝠研究人员和兽医等高危人群进行预暴露 狂犬病,但没有省级强制要求 狂犬病 疫苗。BC省的宠物主人也发现他们对给宠物接种疫苗的兴趣越来越大,一些诊所报告询问量增加了20%。然而,由于错误信息,特别是来自饲养员的错误信息,疫苗 的犹豫仍然存在,许多宠物主人仍然对 狂犬病 疫苗 的必要性感到矛盾。BCCDC 继续调查接触量激增的原因,并建议在可能接触蝙蝠后立即采取行动,包括清洗伤口和寻求医疗护理。

news.content_title: Rabies: This is what every pet owner should know
news.content: Animal rabies occurs in all nine provinces, with dog rabies cycles mainly concentrated in the eastern parts of the country (Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape provinces and the eastern Free State border with Lesotho). Dogs and cats are often moved between provinces by travellers, workers, or holiday-goers, which can easily cause a spillover of rabies to any area if these animals are unvaccinated or inadequately vaccinated and incubating the disease. Remember that any mammal can become infected with rabies, this includes pets, wildlife, livestock and humans. Wildlife species that can host rabies include jackals, foxes, mongooses, aardwolf and Cape fur seals. A map showing reported Rabies outbreaks in South Africa between January 2014 and December 2015. Image: SA Goernment News. If your dogs and cats are vaccinated against rabies, they form a protective barrier for your family and protect you and your beloved pets. The same is true if everyone in your community ensures that their dogs and cats are vaccinated. What is Rabies? Rabies is a fatal disease caused by a virus that can affect all mammals, including humans. The virus is present in high concentrations in the saliva of infected animals and is transmitted by bite wounds. The virus replicates in the tissues, subsequently entering the nerve endings in and around the wound. It can travel along these nerves and gain entry into the central nervous system, rapidly spreading to the brain stem and the forebrain. Typical clinical signs in rabid animals or humans occur once the rabies virus has reached the brain tissue. Once these clinical signs are noted, the disease is usually at a terminal stage and medical intervention is seldom successful. The rabies virus can spread to the salivary glands before the infected animal starts to exhibit symptoms of clinical rabies; the disease can thus be transmitted by infected animals that appear outwardly normal. Image supplied by SA Government News Signs of rabies in dogs and cats: Although signs may vary, infected animals may initially show changes in behaviour, like nervousness and anxiety. These symptoms can last for two or three days. They progress to irritability, photophobia (fear of light), biting, snapping, incoordination and seizures. Some animals may show signs of weakness, incoordination and paralysis, which also affects the muscles used for swallowing. How can you, your dog or cat contract Rabies? Rabies is spread primarily through infected saliva. The virus needs to gain entry into the body, thus normally through an injury to the skin. This usually occurs during a bite wound from a rabid animal. Transmission may also occur if infected saliva comes into contact with open wounds, for example, by licking. What to do if you get bitten by a rabid animal Should you be bitten by a suspected rabid animal, the first step is to wash the wound thoroughly with running water and a disinfectant. You will need to see a doctor immediately so that they can begin post- exposure treatment. (Source: Bayer (Pty) Ltd., Animal Health Division www.bayeranimalhealth.co.za). news.content_original: Animal rabies occurs in all nine provinces, with dog rabies cycles mainly concentrated in the eastern parts of the country (Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape provinces and the eastern Free State border with Lesotho). Dogs and cats are often moved between provinces by travellers, workers, or holiday-goers, which can easily cause a spillover of rabies to any area if these animals are unvaccinated or inadequately vaccinated and incubating the disease. Remember that any mammal can become infected with rabies, this includes pets, wildlife, livestock and humans. Wildlife species that can host rabies include jackals, foxes, mongooses, aardwolf and Cape fur seals. A map showing reported Rabies outbreaks in South Africa between January 2014 and December 2015. Image: SA Goernment News. If your dogs and cats are vaccinated against rabies, they form a protective barrier for your family and protect you and your beloved pets. The same is true if everyone in your community ensures that their dogs and cats are vaccinated. What is Rabies? Rabies is a fatal disease caused by a virus that can affect all mammals, including humans. The virus is present in high concentrations in the saliva of infected animals and is transmitted by bite wounds. The virus replicates in the tissues, subsequently entering the nerve endings in and around the wound. It can travel along these nerves and gain entry into the central nervous system, rapidly spreading to the brain stem and the forebrain. Typical clinical signs in rabid animals or humans occur once the rabies virus has reached the brain tissue. Once these clinical signs are noted, the disease is usually at a terminal stage and medical intervention is seldom successful. The rabies virus can spread to the salivary glands before the infected animal starts to exhibit symptoms of clinical rabies; the disease can thus be transmitted by infected animals that appear outwardly normal. Image supplied by SA Government News Signs of rabies in dogs and cats: Although signs may vary, infected animals may initially show changes in behaviour, like nervousness and anxiety. These symptoms can last for two or three days. They progress to irritability, photophobia (fear of light), biting, snapping, incoordination and seizures. Some animals may show signs of weakness, incoordination and paralysis, which also affects the muscles used for swallowing. How can you, your dog or cat contract Rabies? Rabies is spread primarily through infected saliva. The virus needs to gain entry into the body, thus normally through an injury to the skin. This usually occurs during a bite wound from a rabid animal. Transmission may also occur if infected saliva comes into contact with open wounds, for example, by licking. What to do if you get bitten by a rabid animal Should you be bitten by a suspected rabid animal, the first step is to wash the wound thoroughly with running water and a disinfectant. You will need to see a doctor immediately so that they can begin post- exposure treatment. (Source: Bayer (Pty) Ltd., Animal Health Division www.bayeranimalhealth.co.za). At Caxton, every story is written by humans. We use AI only to perform quality checks - never to generate the news. Happy reading!

(WTOC) - The Liberty County Health Department is urging residents to take precautions after a fox that attacked a local resident tested positive for rabies. The incident happened Monday, Sept. 28, outside a home near Bryant Commons Park in Hinesville. According to health officials, the resident reported being attacked by the animal. The fox was killed and transported to a state public health laboratory, where it tested positive for the deadly virus on Tuesday, Sept. 29. The victim has been notified and is currently receiving post-exposure medical care. Health officials noted that rabies is endemic to coastal Georgia and circulates primarily among wild animals such as raccoons, foxes, and bats. The virus is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear, spreading through bites or scratches from infected animals. Prevention Tips for Residents The Liberty County Health Department’s Environmental Health Office recommends the following safety measures: Avoid unfamiliar animals: Steer clear of wild, stray, or unknown animals, even if they appear friendly. Keep pet vaccinations current: Dogs and cats should receive their initial rabies vaccine after 12 weeks of age, followed by a booster within one year and routine shots every one to three years. Eliminate food sources: Secure outdoor garbage cans and do not leave pet food outside overnight. Do not handle or adopt wildlife: Never bring wild animals into your home or attempt to nurse sick wildlife back to health. Contact local animal control or licensed wildlife rescuers instead. Educate children: Remind kids to “love your own, leave other animals alone.” Signs of rabies in wildlife include uncharacteristic aggression, an unusual lack of fear around humans, sudden behavior changes, paralysis, or foaming at the mouth. Anyone bitten or scratched by an animal should seek immediate medical attention and report the encounter to local animal control and county environmental health officials. Copyright 2026 WTOC. The fox tested positive for rabies at a state public health laboratory on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. The victim, who was bitten or scratched, is currently receiving post-exposure medical care. Health officials warn that rabies is endemic to coastal Georgia and spreads through bites or scratches from infected animals like foxes, raccoons, and bats. The virus is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear. The Liberty County Health Department has advised residents to avoid unfamiliar animals, keep pets vaccinated, and not handle or adopt wildlife. The incident highlights the importance of immediate medical attention and reporting animal encounters to local authorities.

Getty ARA 29/09/2026 - 12:59 h Unverified translation CAT CAST Add us on Google BarcelonaCatalonia has been free of endemic terrestrial rabies for some time, but in recent years there has been growing concern about the airborne transmission of this disease. To the point that the Department of Health has issued a call to the population to avoid contact with bats. It does so as a preventive measure because attacks by these animals—which are currently the main carriers of this disease—are on the rise. During 2026, there have been 23% more attacks in Catalonia by bats compared to those that occurred throughout the previous year. Of the 198 attacks recorded between January 1st and August 12th in the Principality, 86 were carried out by these winged mammals, 16 more than were detected during the entirety of 2025. The rest of the attacks are from dogs. In this case, during the first eight months of the year, one more (56) has been recorded than during all of 2025. Health data show that bat attacks are more frequent during the summer. In the months of June, July, and mid-August alone, almost half of the bites have occurred, 45%. In Catalonia, as in other communities and European countries, the sporadic presence of bats infected with the European rabies virus has been confirmed. A deadly disease Rabies is a very serious disease, almost always fatal, that can affect all mammals. The virus is usually transmitted through the saliva of infected animals through bites, scratches, or licks on open wounds or mucous membranes. In order to prevent infection in people who have suffered an attack by animals considered at risk, the administration of rabies immunoglobulin and the follow-up of a vaccination schedule is necessary, subsequent to the risk exposure. This year, 67% of the exposures reported to the XVEC have required these actions in light of the possibility of contagion. Home Games Sections

news.content: News Issues Wellness Beauty Pharma KOREAN SEARCH Search Health Chosun A Bat Touched His Face, but There Wasn't a Wound... 11-Year-Old Boy Dies By Choi Soo Yeon Updated 2026/07/03 00:30 A case has been reported of an 11-year-old boy who died of rabies after a bat touched his face while he was sleeping./Photo=Getty Images Bank A case has been reported of an 11-year-old boy who died of rabies after a bat touched his face while he was sleeping. On the 30th, local time, the Canadian Medical Association Journal, CMAJ, presented the case to help prevent similar incidents in the future. In the summer of 2024, an 11-year-old boy sleeping at a cottage in Ontario, Canada, found a bat sitting on his nose. Startled, the boy swatted the bat away with his hand. Because there were no visible bite or scratch marks and the bat did not display unusual behavior, his family did not seek medical attention. However, 19 days after coming into contact with the bat, the boy began experiencing numbness and reduced sensation on one side of his face. His face then became swollen and his appetite declined, followed by difficulty swallowing, vomiting, fever, confusion and hallucinations. He was initially mistaken as having a herpesvirus infection and sent home, but when his symptoms worsened the next day, he returned to the hospital. He was ultimately diagnosed with rabies through testing on the fourth day of hospitalization. The boy received treatment in the intensive care unit but died on the 17th day of hospitalization. Rabies can be transmitted when saliva from an infected animal comes into contact not only with a bite wound but also with the mucous membranes of the nose, mouth or eyes, or with an open wound. In this case, too, there were no visible bite marks, but he was presumed to have been infected through this route. ◇ Extremely high fatality rate after symptoms appear Rabies is a fatal infectious disease for which there is virtually no treatment once symptoms appear. It is primarily a zoonotic disease that occurs when the saliva of an animal carrying the rabies virus enters the body through a bite wound, abrasion or mucous membrane. About 99% of human rabies cases are transmitted by dogs, but according to the World Health Organization, in North and South America, where rabies is largely controlled, wild animals such as bats are considered the primary sources of infection. This is the first locally acquired case of rabies in Ontario, Canada, since 1967. Rabies is rare in Canada, with only 28 human cases reported since 1924, but the WHO has reported that tens of thousands of people die from rabies worldwide every year, with children under 15 accounting for about 40% of the victims. No confirmed human rabies cases have been reported in South Korea since 2004. However, rabies virus continues to be detected, particularly in wild raccoons, in areas bordering North Korea, including Incheon, Gyeonggi and Gangwon, prompting disease control authorities to urge people not to let their guard down. If you are bitten by a wild animal or dog suspected of having rabies, or come into direct contact with a bat, you should wash the wound with soap and water for at least 15 minutes and then seek medical attention, even if the wound is small. Most cases of rabies can be prevented by administering post-exposure prophylaxis, PEP, after exposure and before symptoms appear, but it is difficult to expect preventive effects once symptoms have begun. Dr. Brian Hummel, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at McMaster Children's Hospital in Canada, said, “Even if there are no visible bite or scratch marks, post-exposure prophylaxis is necessary if you have had direct contact with a bat,” adding, “This should be kept firmly in mind, especially during the summer, when contact between people and bats increases.” This article has been translated AI. news.content: 24/7 LiveLos AngelesOrange CountyInland EmpireVentura CountyCalifornia 100° HEALTH & FITNESS Record number of rabid bats detected in Los Angeles County Los Angeles County has confirmed 69 rabid bats this year, matching last year's record and prompting public health officials to urge residents to take precautions as peak bat season continues. Tuesday, September 29, 2026 6:01AM Share Follow ABC7 on Google LOS ANGELES (CNS) -- Los Angeles County has confirmed 69 rabid bats this year, matching last year's record and prompting public health officials Monday to urge residents to take precautions as peak bat season continues. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health issued the warning on World Rabies Day, which is observed annually Sept. 28. Rabid bat detections have been trending upward in the county for more than a decade, according to the department. Twenty-four rabid bats were confirmed in August alone, and 32% of bats submitted by residents for rabies testing during the month tested positive. Of the 69 rabid bats detected this year, 68% were found in the Santa Clarita Valley, continuing a trend seen during the past decade. Most were Canyon Bats, suggesting rabies may be circulating more intensely in that local bat population, according to Public Health. "Bats are an important part of our environment, but they can be infected with and spread rabies, a disease that is almost always fatal once symptoms appear," county Health Officer Dr. Muntu Davis said in a statement. "If you find a bat indoors or think you may have had contact with one, contact your medical provider or Public Health right away. And remember, never touch a bat or any wild animals. Immediately report any bat found indoors, or outdoors if it appears sick, active during the day, unable to fly, or dead, to your local animal control." Public Health officials said rabid bats have been found throughout Los Angeles County, including the San Fernando Valley and downtown Los Angeles, and in locations including office buildings, parks, schools, businesses and residential backyards. About one-third of bat encounters occur indoors, where the risk of exposure is higher. Exposure to a rabid bat or a bat that might have rabies can occur when saliva or tissue from the animal enters the body through a bite or scratch, or comes into contact with a wound, mouth, nose or eyes. Because bat bites can be very small and may feel like a pinprick, they can go unnoticed, according to Public Health. Health officials said anyone who wakes up with a bat in the room or finds one near a sleeping person, child or pet should consider it a possible exposure and contact animal control or Public Health. Officials advised residents not to release such bats so they can be safely collected and tested. Rabies can be prevented following an exposure with post-exposure prophylaxis, a series of timely vaccines, according to Public Health. Residents were also urged to keep their pets' rabies vaccinations current, avoid touching bats and other wild animals and report bats that are active during the day, on the ground or unable to fly. news.source_body_en: Los Angeles County has confirmed 69 rabid bats this year, matching last year's record and prompting public health officials to issue warnings on World Rabies Day. The warning, issued on September 29, 2026, urges residents to take precautions, especially as peak bat season continues. Rabid bat detections have been rising for over a decade, with 24 confirmed in August alone and 32% of tested bats testing positive. Of the 69 cases, 68% were found in the Santa Clarita Valley, indicating a localized trend. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health emphasized that bat bites can be unnoticed due to their small size and that rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. Officials advised against touching bats or other wild animals, recommended bat-proofing homes, and urged immediate contact with medical providers or Public Health if a bat is found indoors or near sleeping individuals. Post-exposure prophylaxis is available to prevent rabies following exposure, and residents are encouraged to keep pets' vaccinations up to date. The situation remains under active investigation and management.

supplementary_news.content_title: Iran, WHO join efforts to eliminate human rabies by 2030
supplementary_news.content: About us Membership Contact us Sun October 4, 2026 Home Society Economy Politics Sports Culture International Multimedia Tourism Iran, WHO join efforts to eliminate human rabies by 2030 Society September 29, 2026 - 15:37 TEHRAN – The National Plan for the Elimination of Human Rabies 2026–2030 was formally countersigned at a seminar marking World Rabies Day, hosted by the Ministry of Health and Medical Education's Centre for Communicable Disease Control. The initiative aims to strengthen national efforts to prevent and ultimately eliminate human rabies through coordinated measures in disease surveillance, prevention, public awareness, and timely access to post-exposure treatment. Speaking at the event, Dr Jean Jabbour, WHO Representative in the Islamic Republic of Iran, emphasized the need for collaboration across human health, veterinary services, municipalities, communities and other sectors through a One Health approach. He also highlighted timely care after animal bites and dog vaccination as essential measures to prevent rabies deaths Achieving the goal of zero human deaths from rabies by 2030 requires enhancing collaborations among the health system, veterinary, municipalities, and local communities within the framework of the “One Health” approach, Jabbour stated. Dog bites contribute to 99 percent of human rabies cases. Despite being fatal, rabies is entirely preventable. However, no single organization can defeat the disease on its own, the health ministry’s website quoted Jabbour as saying. The official made the remarks on the occasion of World Rabies Day, which is marked on September 28 every year. Highlighting this year’s World Rabies Day theme, ‘Stronger Together’, he noted that rabies elimination needs ongoing multi-sectoral cooperation among physicians, veterinarians, health staff, municipalities, and local communities. Referring to the number of animal bites in the country, he said over the past two decades there has been a fivefold increase in the number of reported cases. More than 441,000 individuals bitten by animals were referred to medical centers in the past Iranian year (March 2025 – March 2026). Twenty of them lost their lives, and it could have been prevented. Eleven individuals died without receiving any treatment. The statistics indicate that, in addition to prompt presentation of the bitten person to medical centers, timely and appropriate post-exposure care and the raise of public awareness are critical, and every case of animal bite must be treated as a medical emergency. When a person is bitten or scratched by an animal, even if the bite looks small, they have to visit a healthcare provider right away, he added. Noting that approximately four out of every five confirmed rabies deaths in Iran are due to dog bites, Jabbour stated that stray dogs alone account for more than half of these cases, while the rest are attributed to wild animals, including wolves and foxes. The official underlined the role of One Health strategies for rabies control, including constant vaccination of dogs, effective management of stray dogs, and the promotion of close cooperation among the human health, environmental health, and veterinary sectors, he added. Lauding the adopted measures in the country, Jabbour said some 729 rabies prevention and treatment centers are operating across the country, and post-exposure care services are provided in all provinces. Around one million doses of human rabies vaccine and 180,000 vials of anti-rabies serum are procured for the national program, annually; Pasteur Institute of Iran helps diagnose confirmed cases of rabies as well as train physicians and health workers. The official went on to say that the development of a national strategic document for rabies eradication is also a significant step toward aligning Iran with the global goal of “zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030”, adding that the WHO is committed to supporting Iran, through technical assistance and collaboration, in achieving the goal. Why “Stronger Together”? The 2026 theme, ‘Stronger Together’, highlights a simple truth: rabies elimination is only possible when we work together. Expand access to life-saving dog vaccinations. Improve rabies surveillance and reporting systems. Strengthen public awareness and education. Support policies that protect both people and animals. Build sustainable community-led solutions. Rabies elimination depends on connected systems. Stronger partnerships create stronger outcomes! We all have a role to play From local communities and veterinary professionals to governments, healthcare workers, educators, and global partners, we all have role to play in making a world free from rabies a reality. Communities: Communities are often the first line of defense against rabies. Education, awareness, and responsible animal care help prevent cases before they happen. Veterinary Professionals: Mass dog vaccination remains the most effective way to stop rabies at its source. Healthcare Workers: Timely treatment and accurate diagnosis save lives. Governments and Policymakers: Strong legislation, investment, and national coordination are essential for long-term progress. Global Partners: Collaboration across sectors helps share resources, expertise, and solutions that accelerate impact. One Health in action Rabies elimination depends on interconnected action. Education, vaccination, surveillance, and legislation cannot work in isolation, they must function as part of one coordinated system. World Rabies Day 2026 reinforces the importance of a One Health approach, recognizing the connection between human, animal, and environmental health. supplementary_news.content: Skip to contentMenuToday's paper Long IslandSportsNewsInvestigationsRestaurantsOpinionBusinessThings to DoSchoolsObitsNewsday TVSearchTOGETHER LI HealthYankees in ALDSHalloween events on LITop 50 best restaurantsWallet Watch NewsHealthOnly in Newsday Rabies is spreading in LI's raccoons, and workers are responding with vaccine bait A raccoon at an undisclosed Suffolk County location feeds on oral rabies vaccine bait. Credit: Suffolk County Department of Health Services By Lisa L. Colangelolisa.colangelo@newsday.com@lisalcolangeloUpdated October 3, 2026 5:22 pm Share Raccoons will eat just about anything, especially if it's covered with cod liver oil and fish meal crumbles. That’s what health officials on Long Island are hoping, as workers distribute hundreds of thousands of fish-flavored packets containing rabies vaccine in wooded areas, culverts and other places raccoons like to gather. Vaccine baiting for raccoons is an important weapon against a wildlife rabies outbreak that started in Nassau County in 2024 and spread into Suffolk County last year. Since February 2025, 51 cases of terrestrial rabies have been documented in Suffolk County — in 49 raccoons and two cats. Before that, there had not been a case since 2009, officials said. Terrestrial rabies cases do not include bats, which also carry the virus. WHAT NEWSDAY FOUND The local outbreak of terrestrial wildlife rabies on Long Island, which includes raccoons and some cats, has been moving farther into Suffolk County in recent months. Health officials are placing rabies vaccine baits, flavored with fish, to attract raccoons. Once they bite the bait, the vaccine will enter their system and provide protection from the virus. Residents are warned to stay away from wildlife and make sure their pets have updated rabies vaccines. Pets are an important barrier between the virus in wildlife and people. Oral rabies vaccine baits, covered in cod liver oil and other substances, that were distributed by the Nassau County Department of Health. Credit: Credit: Nassau County Department of Health Most of the cases were clustered in Amityville, with a few in Lindenhurst, Deer Park and Wyandanch. But over the past few months, they also have been found farther east and north in Babylon, Bay Shore, Islip, Northport, Smithtown and Kings Park. Sign up for the Health newsletter Get the latest stories every week about health and wellness, covering topics from medicine and mental health to updates on the coronavirus and new research. Sign up By clicking Sign up, you agree to our privacy policy. A raccoon picked up in Manorville in June after an encounter with a local resident tested positive for rabies. Health officials believe it likely was relocated from another area since its location was far from where other raccoons with rabies were found. Preventive measures With surveillance, vaccine baits and free rabies shots for pets, Suffolk County is trying to hold the line. Rabies is a potentially deadly virus that is transmitted via the saliva of an infected animal. That can happen through a bite or by the infected saliva getting into an open wound, eyes, nose or mouth, according to the state Health Department. While fatal human cases of rabies are rare — the last one in New York State was more than 30 years ago and involved an encounter with a bat — they also can be avoided with prompt medical treatment. Suffolk County already has distributed about 240,000 vaccine bait packets, and Nassau will put out more than 144,000 by Oct. 9. “The goal of the bait program is to provide herd immunity,” said Dr. Meghan Davis, a veterinarian and chair of the master of public health program at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “But you are not going to catch every member of the herd. ... It’s about serving as a line of defense.” The vaccine baits are making a difference, Suffolk County Health Commissioner Dr. Gregson Pigott told Newsday. He said U.S. Department of Agriculture staff trapped and tested blood from numerous raccoons in the areas that were baited last year to determine the effectiveness of the program. The tests showed 26% of raccoons showed an antibody response, above the average of 10%-15% that the USDA typically finds following a first-time baiting program. Staying away from wildlife is the best way to avoid any kind of illness, state officials said, advising people to contact a rehabilitator if they believe an animal is sick or injured. If a person or pet is in contact with or bitten by a wild animal, they should seek immediate medical treatment and contact their county's health department. Companion dogs, cats and ferrets must be vaccinated against rabies under New York State law, the first shot no later than four months after birth and the second within a year later. Booster shots are required at different intervals, one year or three years, depending on the animal and vaccine. Vaccinating pets Davis pointed out that while the baiting program is designed to reduce how many wild animals become rabid and infectious, dog and cat vaccines protect people by providing a shield for the animals most likely to infect them. “Especially if you live on Long Island,” said Dr. Carly Fox, senior veterinarian for urgent and emergency care at the Schwarzman Animal Medical Center in Manhattan. “If you let your dog outside or if you have a cat that goes outside, they can experience interactions with wildlife that you just don't witness.” In two separate Kings Park incidents, dogs and their owners came in contact with raccoons that later tested positive for rabies. The dogs had been previously vaccinated against rabies and received booster shots. The individuals were treated for exposure. Both counties have held several free rabies vaccination clinics for pets since the first cases of the local outbreak were discovered in Nassau County in 2024. The cases included four raccoons and two stray cats. A Suffolk County Department of Health Services employee distributes vaccine baits in Suffolk County last month. Credit: Suffolk County Department of Hea In early 2025, as cases started to rise, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman suggested raccoons with rabies may have crossed over from Queens because New York City did not perform rabies vaccine baiting in 2024. The city Health Department said it didn't have the funding that year to continue the program but also said there is no way to determine "how and where rabid raccoons are moving or being moved by people." It also pointed out there was rabies vaccine distribution in southwestern Nassau County in September 2024. Nassau and Suffolk started active surveillance programs, testing raccoons that were found dead or appeared sickly or disoriented. Since raccoons have acclimated well to urban and suburban environments, seeing them during the day foraging for food is common and not a sign they are ill. The number of terrestrial wildlife rabies cases in Nassau jumped to 27 in 2025 — 26 raccoons and one stray cat — and has dropped to one raccoon so far this year. In a statement announcing the latest round of baiting, Nassau Health Commissioner Dr. Irina Gelman called the decline in confirmed rabies cases “encouraging.” “Following the return of rabies in 2024, NCDOH implemented extensive rabies control efforts, including an expanded oral rabies vaccine baiting program to help vaccinate raccoons and other terrestrial wildlife against the virus,” she said. “Those highly successful efforts have continued.” Occasional outbreaks These local outbreaks generally last from one to two years, followed by a decline in the raccoon population due to deaths from the virus, the state Health Department said. The population rebounds in about five years, sometimes causing “periodic flare-ups” of rabies. The dynamics of exposure between humans and raccoons are changing and becoming more challenging, especially with people who feed colonies of stray cats every day, said Gary Whittaker, a professor of virology at the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine. Those caretakers are in contact with cats that sometimes end up sharing resources with raccoons — putting them at risk of contracting rabies, he said. “People want to take care of the cats and they put out food for the cats, and the raccoons are taking advantage of that,” he said. “It’s also allowing an increase in the raccoon population.” Whittaker was one of the authors of a study that examined how raccoons in Brooklyn's Green-Wood Cemetery acclimate to the environment and interact with other animals. “They are incredibly successful, smart animals,” he said. “We’ve got pictures of a raccoon and a cat sharing the same food bowl, side by side.” By Lisa L. Colangelo lisa.colangelo@newsday.com@lisalcolangelo Lisa joined Newsday as a staff writer in 2019. She previously worked at amNewYork, the New York Daily News and the Asbury Park Press covering politics, government and general assignment.
